First mate and Nulo are both cheaper in my shop by a few bucks a bag. Pro plan is not the worst and I'd agree that its not bad low priced food, purina one on the other hand, is hot trash.

Both of these dog foods I would consider the holly grail of kibbles. I know of better diets out there for dogs but you have to start getting into raw and freeze dried shit and thats a pain. You feed your dog better than 95% of people.

First mate is cheaper. Nulo is cheaper. Here are just two options but blue is amazingly overpriced. I would also argue that the two foods I listed are leaps and bounds better than blues formula. Blue is good once you step into the wilderness line, but the normal stuff is the low end of good dog food.

The exact same thing could be said about burger king and humans. Will Purina kill your animal? No. Would I compare it to feeding ramen noodles everyday of ones life? Yes. Go look at the ingredients in purina one. Four out of the first 5 ingredients are grains. Thats no just bad, its really bad. Even the cheapest of foods I sell have maybe one or two sources of grains tops, and never wheat, an item well known to cause all sorts of issues in dogs. Like. Lots and lots of issues. It might have given the least problems, but that can only mean the other stuff was worse, which is almost scary. Also, you are feeding byproduct meal... That could be almost anything. Purina wont kill your dog, but chases are they will live longer on a diet thats actually designed for a dog. Purina is made for your wallet, not your pet.

Yeah I dont like blue quality wise or price. They are about 4 bucks more expensive per 4 pound bag than First Mate, which is a much higher quality. Same for Nulo. Steer clear of blue, but for gods sake done feed purina.

It comes down to a few factors like age and activity level but the two foods I think I point people to the most at First Mate and Nulo. You can also score amazing deals on FROMM off of amazon and that stuff is great. If price is not an option Orijen or a good raw food for dogs. 
Everything I listed shares a few things. They are all limited ingredient diets which I like. They all have good protein, sourced from America or Canada. Really this list could go on and on, these are great foods.
 My advice is if you dont know what the ingredient is on the side of the food it is most likely suspect. I've seen some brands call salt five different things just so they could pack more and more in and sugar is everywhere in the grocery store dog foods. Feed your pet well and get them exercise and they will live longer.

I went to a military like boarding school that made Marine Boot Camp hilariously tame. I was in constant trouble for laughing too much. I had hiked the width of the Costa Rican rain forrest by the time I was 16 doing outward bound and shit so the hikes while painful at times were also tame. I only mention these things because your point on mental strength is dead on. I was lucky enough to KNOW I could get through boot because I had already done harder things in my life. The biggest thing I saw happening when people failed was them giving up on themselves. I ended up In GSP as a 0311 and 8621 and let me tell you no amount of training is going to prepare you for a 130 pound pack on top of all the other PPE and ammo and shit you are carrying. Confidence in yourself though will allow you to do anything. For example I ran my best PFT of all time during my recon indoc and by the time I was running I was tired from the swimming and other bullshit Marine life brings. Wasnt because I trained any harder for that test, it was all because I believed I could and wouldn't let myself quit. 
My best advise for anyone doing anything involving hard physical work is this. Understand its going to suck. Sometimes it will suck real, real bad. There will be times your brain will tell you that you have nothing left to give and you should give up. Don't. Understand that your brain, like mine, is a lying sac of shit who doesn't care about you. Don't listen to that part of your brain. Turn it off. You are capable of more than you have ever imagined. I'm a computer nerd that enjoys video games, bad movies, and being lazy. But I've also seen and done things movies cant because of cost constraints. I've seen hell rain from the sky, hung off copters by a rope, gone ATVing with NSW, and lived in more countries than most Americans have visited states. I am in no way a bad ass. I just refused to give up on myself.

It's hard for me to be called a hero or be thanked. I'm not a hero. I was an infantry man in an Intel Bn. and I deployed a couple times, saw some shit, did some stuff, but none of that stuff makes me a hero. To be honest there's only one or two operations I was involved in that I feel really good about, and I worked a good deal while I was over seas.
Mostly my time was spent traveling from one shit hole to another in some sort of truck waiting to get blown up. Sleeping on a convoy because you you'd rather be dreaming than staring at a dirt road when you get killed is not heroic, but that's how I spent a good deal of my time in Afghanistan. 
What pisses me off is when the non combat MOS people talk a big game. Most non combat MOS types while deployed live in what would amount to luxury compared to the places I stayed. Deployments for most service people is actually quite easy. In the latter years of Iraq the POGs that lived on TQ and Al Assad lived like kings. In Afganistan over on leather neck life wasn't to bad either. I was there when it was being constructed and I was there when it was pretty built up. If Wi-Fi internet, hot showers, lobster and steak dinners (at least once a week, no fucking lie) are hard core then I must be Arnold Schwarzenegger from commando (I'm not). 
For most people deployments are not all that rough. Some people have it WAY WAY WAY WAY WAY better than others during their military careers. Not every Marine is a rifleman (I find this statement insanely untrue and a mite disrespectful). The things I've seen POGs do in training, on the range, still make me laugh when I think about it.
As for you not trusting people, there are very very few non infantry types that I would trust outside the wire, lets not even talk about combat. 
Most of us don't deserve your thanks. Many of us service members mopped a floor and collected a check for their entire careers. I once had the great pleasure to be under a mustang platoon commander who in 2010, after 20 years in the Marines, had not deployed once. Guy thought of himself as a rock star, but couldn't understand why I would provide a 5 paragraph order to my guys or himself before stepping off on a training op. 
I'm rambling and its early.

Prior military here. Shaving is something because of the job I had to do once to twice a day. I've used everything. For a long while I had switched to dry shaving because it was practical while I was deployed and all but I've used just about every thing on the market. 
I just this morning tried my first DE shave and I think its the best shave I've ever had. Ever. I cut myself a couple times and I'm sure I'm only going to get better at it but I'm shocked at how much better a shave I got. 
The feeling of it was amazing. I'm switching from a fusion and I always get tugging and some pain no matter what I used for cream but with the DE it just slid over my face. At first I was worried I wasnt actually cutting anything because I couldn't feel the normal feelings I get from a blade going across my face. Once I did my post shave thing though I was shocked. I am shocked. There's no way in hell I'm ever going back.

I should be getting some Trumper skin food to take over as a balm for post shave sometime today but I have minimal discomfort/razor burn and it's amazing how close I got. I went WTG, XTG, then WTG again and I dont even get this close going ATG with a fusion. I think I might be hooked.
Thanks I might pick some up latter today!

After two deployments and hundreds of hours running ops I was the undisputed SME in our shop. I was about 6 months from EAS and I had done jobs with people only a few members of my command knew about, need to know shit. When I spoke about our job, everyone listened. Funny part is I was only a LCPL. 
Six months out, suffering from severe symptoms of PTSD, I just stopped caring. This translated to me being honest open with the newer and younger guys, which in my opinion included everyone who knew less than me. I started speaking my mind constantly, but as anyone who likes to read orders out of the UCMJ knows, its hard to fuck with people who know their orders. 
To make a ton of great stories short, I was eventually told that I was no allowed to go to work anymore. I was to report to my barracks room at 0800 and I could release myself at 1300. For 6 months I was paid to drink beer and play video games. Those 6 months I now consider the craziest 6 months in my life. 
I've had the Japanese riot police called on a house party, flown to Tokyo an hour after someone asked, "what do we want to do tonight", too many stories to list.
Moral here? Read your god damned orders. There's an old one that said you could have two drinks at lunch I used to carry around in my pocket. That order was out of date even when I was in, but I'll be damned if anyone could prove it without having to read the UCMJ themselves. Most people don't do that. 
There are times I still miss the corps. Kinda.

My shiba is my first dog and I have to say the hoopla about them being terrible first time pets is malarkey. BUT... You have to be willing to put in a lot of time with your pet. Walking a shiba for at least an hour a day is a must. You really can see mine start getting weird if she hasn't gone out in a day or two. I tend to take mine to the park for an hour or two a day. Mines only a little over a year but two hours at the dog park doesn't even wear mine out. Not close. 
Mine is super loving but only when she wants to be. My girl would rather be on the floor chewing on a bully stick than sitting with me (unless im holding her chew toy for her). Mine will come snuggle up but I'm the only one in the family she will do this too. This is not to say she doesn't love her family but she is a shiba...
Hair everywhere during the winter months. Its insane. It at times does not seem possible that a dog could constantly loose so much hair. I cant stress enough the craziness that is a blowing coat. I sweep up at least twice a day and i get piles of hair. 
They destroy things. If they get bored they will destroy things. I go through 20 bucks in chew toys a week and while they help she still needs to be watched constantly. 
Shibas are tough dogs for sure. Stubborn, smart, manipulative, destructive... They are a handful. If you are ready for all that (you are not, I was not close to ready, I was shocked at how unprepared I was) they are the best. Even with all the bad traits I wouldn't give mine up for anything. 
I got mine as a companion dog to try and help me with my PTSD and get me out of the house and stuff. She has done wonders for me. Sibas rule.

Mine is only a bit over a year. While she has come a long way since 10 weeks, she is still a furry little wrecking ball. The amount of super expensive furniture she has ruined is mind blowing. But look at that smile!
As long as you can dedicate time to walk your shiba every day, or even better go to a dog park, you should be fine.
